what: Box sells cloud storage and content management to companies. Files live in Box rather than on a shared drive, with permissions, audit trails, retention rules and electronic signatures around them, which is what regulated industries need and a consumer file-sharing service does not provide.
customers: Large and mid-sized organisations, particularly in regulated industries — financial services, healthcare, government and legal — where who opened which document and when is a compliance question.
money: Annual contracts priced per user, with higher tiers adding security, governance, electronic signature and workflow features.
moat: Once a company’s documents, permissions and retention policies live in Box, moving them is a migration project nobody volunteers for, and the compliance certifications Box holds take years to obtain. The customer is the chief information officer rather than an individual employee, which makes the relationship contractual and sticky.
risks: Microsoft bundles SharePoint and OneDrive into subscriptions customers already pay for, which is the hardest competitive problem in software: beating free.
Growth is slow — revenue went from $1.1B to $1.2B — so the thesis has to be margin and cash flow rather than expansion.
The shares trade at about 63 times earnings, because share-based compensation consumes most of the accounting profit.
Debt of $556.1M against $478.1M of cash reflects a convertible issue; dilution is a real cost to shareholders even when it is not a cash cost.
Seven analysts average a $47.29 target, under 10% above the current price.
opportunities: Free cash flow of $389.2M against a $5.9B market value is a 6.6% yield, and the shares trade at about 15 times free cash flow.
Regulated industries will not put sensitive documents in a general-purpose consumer tool, which is the durable reason Box exists alongside Microsoft.
Higher-priced tiers with governance, electronic signature and workflow raise revenue per customer without adding customers.
Buybacks funded by the cash flow have been steadily shrinking the share count against flat revenue.
watch: Revenue per customer and the share on higher tiers. Box cannot win on seats against Microsoft; it can only win by charging more for each one, and that figure shows whether it is.
view: Box has spent a decade in the hardest position in enterprise software: selling something Microsoft gives away. SharePoint and OneDrive are bundled into subscriptions that almost every corporate customer already pays for, and beating free requires being genuinely, demonstrably better at something specific. Box’s answer is governance — permissions, audit trails, retention policies and compliance certifications that let a bank or a hospital put regulated documents somewhere and prove who touched them. That is a real answer, and it is why Box still exists.

It is not, however, an answer that produces growth. Revenue has moved from $1.1 billion to $1.2 billion, and anyone buying this for expansion is buying the wrong stock. What they would be buying instead is $389 million of free cash flow against a $5.9 billion market value — about 15 times free cash flow, with the company steadily retiring shares. That is a perfectly respectable way to make money from a no-growth business, provided the revenue holds.

The 63 times earnings figure is the usual software accounting problem and should be set aside: share-based compensation eats the reported profit while the cash arrives regardless. But it should not be set aside entirely, because the compensation is dilution, and dilution is a genuine transfer from shareholders to employees. The buyback is partly just offsetting it. Judge the share count, not the buyback announcement.

Where I land is that this is a fairly priced, cash-generative business with a defensible niche and a permanent ceiling. The ceiling is Microsoft, and it is not going anywhere. The way Box grows from here is by charging existing customers more — higher tiers with governance, signature and workflow — rather than by winning new seats, which it mostly cannot. Revenue per customer is the number that tells you whether that is working. If it rises, this compounds quietly. If it flattens, you own a melting asset at 15 times cash flow, which is roughly fair and not much more.
bull: Higher-priced governance and workflow tiers raise revenue per customer while buybacks shrink the share count, and a 15 times free cash flow multiple compounds quietly.
bear: Microsoft’s bundled tools are good enough for more customers each year, seat counts slip, and a no-growth business at 15 times cash flow turns into a declining one.
